sweep_summary: Only one title-works with stress in the title (Morén 2000), already the catalog's deciding source. Its author preprint ROA-273 was downloaded from the Rutgers Optimality Archive (link recovered from ROA.xlsx after the guessed URLs 404ed) and read: the catalog quotation is verbatim (pp. 4-6), weight coding confirmed, all data from Bhatt 1989 ms. Beyond the list: Munshi & Crowhurst 2012 remains closed (Crossref abstract. it independently reports weight-driven stress on first-hand Srinagar data, priority high); new first-hand descriptive statement found in Kelkar 1984 (Aspects of Kashmiri Linguistics p. 69: 'no word accent.. automatic light stress on the initial syllable'), which contradicts the weight coding and is the primary form of the SPA/Kelkar & Trisal 1964 line; Koul & Wali 2006 (p. 15-16), Koul 2005 (p. 12) and Koul 2000 say stress is non-distinctive and give no placement rule; Bailey 1937 uses stressed/unstressed vowel allophony but states no rule; Grierson 1895 (JRAS) does not cover Kashmiri; Wade 1888, Koul 2006 course and the LSI extract are silent. catalog's classification 'weight' stands; the record's caution line should cite Kelkar 1984 p. 69 directly. Still unread: Bhatt 1989 ms (medium), Kelkar & Trisal 1964, Wali & Koul 1997, Rosenthall & van der Hulst 1999 (low).org APIs.

new_statements.quote: There is no word accent (as in English) or word tone (as in Panjabi) in Kashmiri. There is an automatic light stress on the initial syllable of a word. At the sentence level, Kashmiri probably has word-final, sentence-medial, and sentence-final junctures; sentence accents; and sentence tones. But all these remain to be properly studied.
new_statements.citation: Kelkar, Ashok R. 1984. Kashmiri: a descriptive sketch. In Omkar N. Koul & Peter Edwin Hook (eds.), Aspects of Kashmiri Linguistics (SILL 12), 62-89. New Delhi: Bahri Publications.
new_statements.locator: p. 69, 'Sentence Phonology' (djvu the text layer; running heads 'Kashmiri : A Descriptive Sketch 69' and '70 Kashmiri Linguistics')
new_statements.reading: The only first-hand descriptive statement of placement read in this search of works with stress in the title: stress is non-contrastive and falls automatically (lightly) on the initial syllable, with no weight sensitivity mentioned. It is the primary form of the Kelkar & Trisal 1964 claim that the record so far held only through the SPA 1979 abstract. It contradicts the weight coding but is a one-sentence remark in a sketch that defers prosody to future study; the weight coding rests on Bhatt 1989's polysyllabic data as restated verbatim in Morén ROA-273 (now obtained, confirmed) and is independently supported by the first-hand Srinagar study of Munshi & Crowhurst 2012 (abstract: 'describes and analyses the pattern of word stress.. CVːC>CVː>CVC>CV'). Note that for words whose non-final syllables are all light, Morén/Bhatt also predict initial stress, so Kelkar's statement is consistent with the default case.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: verbatim in held ROA-273 text/PDF pp. 4-6 exactly as the locator says. (2) Deciding source is a 2000 theoretical phonology article restating an unpublished 1989 ms; not the best available. The best available, Munshi & Crowhurst 2012 (J. Ling., 46 pp., first-hand Srinagar data), is held only as an abstract, but that abstract independently states the CVːC > CVː > CVC > CV weight scale and weight-driven stress, so the 'weight / leftmost heaviest non-final / CVV+CVC / unbounded' coding is very unlikely to flip. (3) Two descriptive-tradition sources disagree in kind rather than in detail: Kelkar & Trisal 1964 (via SPA 1979, downloaded now) say accent is non-contrastive and phonetically always initial, and the held Koul & Wali 2006 grammar says stress is not distinctive and gives no rule; Handoo 1973 (downloaded now) explicitly declines to describe stress. sources.citation: Morén, Bruce. 2000. The puzzle of Kashmiri stress: implications for weight theory. Phonology 17(3): 365-396. DOI 10.1017/S0952675701003967. Author preprint: ROA-273 (1998, 24 pp.).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: All data are taken from Bhatt (1989). ... As (13) shows, in monomorphemic disyllabic words, the final syllable is never stressed, regardless of weight. ... However, in words of more than two syllables, stress is determined by syllable weight. In words containing long vowels, the leftmost, non-final, long vowel is stressed. ... In the absence of a long vowel, the leftmost non-final closed syllable is stressed. ... Non-final closed syllables containing long vowels (superheavy) are stressed in preference to all other syllables. ... Finally, stress is assigned to the initial syllable if all non-final syllables are light. ... main stress in Kashmiri is as far left in a word as possible. However, it is weight sensitive, and retracts to the left-most heaviest syllable of the word (excluding final syllables).
sources.locator: ROA-273 sec. 2.2 'Stress', pp. 4-6 (the text layer); Phonology version pp. 365-396 not yet obtained
sources.note: Unbounded weight-sensitive stress: leftmost non-final CVːC > leftmost non-final CVː > leftmost non-final CVC > initial; final syllable never stressed; long vowel wins over a closed syllable to its left. All data second-hand from Bhatt 1989 ms. The ROA text is verbatim the catalog quotation.

sources.quote: This paper describes and analyses the pattern of word stress found in the standard dialect of Koshur (Kashmiri) spoken in Srinagar. ... its pattern of stress assignment and a pervasive pattern of syncope conspire to produce a four-way syllable weight distinction that has sometimes been expressed as the scale CVːC>CVː>CVC>CV. ... closed syllables, CVːC and CVC are preferred as stress peaks over open syllables with vowels of the same length. ... In a stress clash context however, CVC defers to CVː.
sources.locator: Crossref abstract (publisher landing page is /abs/, closed; Semantic Scholar CLOSED; OpenAlex no OA location)
sources.note: The only dedicated first-hand description+analysis of Kashmiri word stress (native-speaker author, Srinagar standard dialect, 46 pp.); our classification rests on Morén's restatement of an unpublished 1989 ms. The full text would settle final-syllable extrametricality, the CVC-vs-CVː tie-break, secondary stress (we code 'none reported') and the syncope interaction the abstract mentions.
